Safeworld launches human simulation for robot safety testing

The startup emerges with more than $12 million in seed funding to test how robots respond to unpredictable human encounters.

TechCrunch ↗5 October 2026English editorial summary
StoryImages 1

A launch focused on deployment risk

Safeworld emerged on October 5 with more than $12 million in seed funding led by Shine Capital and a16z Speedrun. Its founders are Carnegie Mellon Safe AI researcher Ding Zhao, Kyle Wong and Simo Rachidi. Their premise is that generative robot controllers require evaluation of variable behavior, beyond checking whether a machine follows a fixed instruction.

Simulating people around working robots

The company recreates settings such as factory blind corners in tools including Genesis or MuJoCo, then runs the robot’s actual control software against simulated human encounters. Scenarios can involve people carrying boxes, kneeling, running or falling. Gritt Robotics, which develops robots for construction and solar installations, is collaborating on these safety simulations.

Testing is not a blanket safety guarantee

Operators still need to understand how well test scenarios represent their own sites and how findings inform speed, stopping distances and operating limits. Simulation can expose weaknesses without putting people at risk, but cannot establish safety in every possible situation. Safeworld is still considering a platform versus services model; the launch is not a completed certification scheme.
